subject: history

questions.content: Which name is given to the laws in the southern United States that enforced racial segregation after the Civil War?
questions.explanation: Jim Crow laws separated Black and white Americans in schools, transport and public places, and often denied Black people the vote.

questions.content: The 1954 Supreme Court case Brown v. Board of Education ruled that:
options: Schools could choose their own racial policies
questions.explanation: The Court ruled that separate schools for Black and white children were inherently unequal, overturning 'separate but equal' in education.

questions.content: Whose arrest in December 1955 sparked the Montgomery Bus Boycott?
questions.explanation: Rosa Parks was arrested for refusing to give up her bus seat to a white passenger, and the boycott began soon after.

questions.content: Martin Luther King Jr. delivered his 'I Have a Dream' speech at which 1963 event?
questions.explanation: About 250,000 people gathered in Washington D.C. on 28 August 1963 to demand jobs and civil rights.

questions.content: Which law of 1965 removed barriers such as literacy tests that stopped Black Americans voting?
questions.explanation: The Voting Rights Act of 1965 outlawed discriminatory voting tests and allowed federal supervision of registration.

questions.content: The Montgomery Bus Boycott lasted 381 days. What made it successful?
options: Black residents, who made up most of the bus passengers, organised carpools and kept up the boycott, hurting bus company income
The boycott was violent and frightened the city
The state governor ordered an end to segregation
questions.explanation: The loss of fares combined with a Supreme Court ruling against bus segregation ended the policy in December 1956.

questions.content: In 1957 nine Black students attempted to attend Central High School in Little Rock, Arkansas. President Eisenhower sent federal troops. What did this show?
options: The federal government would enforce desegregation orders against state resistance
The students were not allowed to attend
questions.explanation: The state governor tried to block the students, so Eisenhower sent the 101st Airborne to protect them and enforce the court ruling.

questions.content: In February 1960 four Black students sat at a whites-only lunch counter in Greensboro, North Carolina, and refused to leave. Which tactic was this?
questions.explanation: Sit-ins spread quickly across the South and led to the formation of the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee (SNCC).

questions.content: How did the Birmingham campaign of 1963 help to produce the Civil Rights Act of 1964?
options: Television images of police using dogs and fire hoses on peaceful protesters shocked national opinion
It removed the need for a law
It was ignored by the media
questions.explanation: The images of violence against peaceful marchers, including children, increased support for federal action. President Kennedy proposed new civil rights legislation.

questions.content: A fictional county had 10,000 Black residents of voting age in 1964, of whom 200 were registered. After the Voting Rights Act, 6,500 were registered. By how many percentage points did the registered share rise?
questions.explanation: Before: 200 ÷ 10,000 = 2%. After: 6,500 ÷ 10,000 = 65%. The rise is 65 − 2 = 63 percentage points.

questions.content: Which pair correctly matches a civil rights leader or group with its approach?
options: Martin Luther King Jr. – non-violent protest
Malcolm X – the March on Washington organiser in 1963
The Black Panthers – supported Jim Crow
questions.explanation: King led the Southern Christian Leadership Conference and promoted non-violence. Malcolm X and the Black Panthers advocated more militant self-defence and Black pride.

questions.content: A historian says: 'The movement succeeded because ordinary people took action.' Another says: 'It succeeded because the federal government and courts intervened.' What is the best description of this difference?
options: One stresses change from below and the other change from above
One is primary and the other is secondary
One is accurate and the other is false
One discusses the USA and the other discusses the UK
questions.explanation: A balanced explanation combines grassroots action, such as boycotts and marches, with decisions made by courts and Congress.

questions.content: Which organisation, founded in 1909, used lawsuits and the courts as its main route to challenge segregation, including in Brown v. Board of Education?
questions.explanation: The National Association for the Advancement of Colored People pursued legal challenges, while groups like SNCC and SCLC organised direct action.

questions.content: In 1964 Malcolm X said Black people should defend themselves 'by any means necessary'. How did his approach differ from Martin Luther King's?
options: He emphasised self-defence and Black pride and was more critical of integration
questions.explanation: The phrase was real and part of a wider debate. Malcolm X's approach contrasted with King's non-violent integration strategy, although his views developed before his assassination in 1965.

questions.content: The Civil Rights Act of 1964 outlawed segregation in public places and discrimination in employment, yet the Voting Rights Act was needed in 1965. Why?
options: Black Americans in the South still faced obstacles to voting, such as literacy tests and intimidation
Black Americans did not want to vote
The 1964 Act applied only to the north
questions.explanation: The 1964 Act did not remove voting barriers. The Selma marches of 1965 drew attention to this and encouraged Congress to act.

questions.content: After 1965, many Black Americans in northern cities felt laws had not improved poverty, housing or policing. Which development reflects this frustration?
options: The growth of Black Power and urban riots such as Watts in 1965
The repeal of the Civil Rights Act
The reintroduction of Jim Crow laws
questions.explanation: Legal equality did not remove economic inequality. The Watts riots in Los Angeles in August 1965 and Black Power movement showed this dissatisfaction.

questions.content: Which statement best evaluates the importance of the Montgomery Bus Boycott?
options: It was important for showing the power of mass non-violent action and bringing Martin Luther King Jr. to national attention, though it was one stage among many
It happened after the Civil Rights Act
questions.explanation: It was a turning point but not the sole cause of change. Strong answers justify significance and acknowledge limits.

questions.content: A photograph of the 1963 March on Washington shows a huge peaceful crowd. What is a limitation of using it alone to judge the march's impact?
options: It shows the scale and mood but not the political results or the views of those who opposed it
It was taken in the wrong year
questions.explanation: A photo is strong evidence of attendance and atmosphere, but it needs other sources to show consequences.

note:
## Background: segregation
After the Civil War (1861–65) slavery was abolished and the Fourteenth Amendment promised equal protection of the law. In the South, however, Jim Crow laws enforced segregation in schools, transport and public places. The 1896 Supreme Court case Plessy v. Ferguson allowed 'separate but equal' facilities, which in practice were unequal. Many Black Americans were also prevented from voting by literacy tests and intimidation.

## Key events and stages
- **Brown v. Board of Education (1954).** The Supreme Court ruled that segregated schools were unconstitutional.
- **Montgomery Bus Boycott (1955–56).** After Rosa Parks was arrested on 1 December 1955, Black residents boycotted buses for 381 days, using carpools and walking. The Supreme Court ruled bus segregation unlawful. Martin Luther King Jr. became a national figure.
- **Little Rock (1957).** Nine Black students tried to attend Central High School. When the state governor resisted, President Eisenhower sent federal troops to enforce desegregation.
- **Sit-ins and Freedom Rides (1960–61).** Students in Greensboro began sit-ins at lunch counters. The Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee (SNCC) was formed. Freedom Riders challenged segregation on interstate buses and were attacked.
- **Birmingham (1963).** Police used dogs and fire hoses on peaceful protesters, including children, and television images shocked the nation.
- **March on Washington (28 August 1963).** About 250,000 people gathered, and King delivered his 'I Have a Dream' speech.
- **Legislation.** The Civil Rights Act (1964) banned segregation in public places and discrimination in employment. The Voting Rights Act (1965), passed after the marches at Selma, removed discriminatory voting tests.

## Different approaches
Organisations included the NAACP (using courts), the Southern Christian Leadership Conference (non-violent mass action) and SNCC (youth activism). Malcolm X, a leader in the Nation of Islam, argued for Black pride and self-defence, and the Black Panthers formed in 1966. Malcolm X was assassinated in 1965 and King on 4 April 1968 in Memphis. Many northern cities still faced poverty and discrimination, leading to riots such as Watts in 1965.

## Why did the movement succeed?
Factors include courageous mass action, strong organisations, media coverage, Supreme Court decisions and presidents who supported legislation. Weaknesses included resistance from southern states, violence by groups such as the Ku Klux Klan, and slow economic change.

## Common mistakes
- Writing as if one person, such as King, achieved everything.
- Mixing up the Civil Rights Act (1964) and the Voting Rights Act (1965).
- Treating the movement as only non-violent. There were different views.

## How this is examined
In the eAssessment you may be given an extract, such as a speech, a news report or a photograph description, and asked about its origin, purpose, value and limitation. Longer tasks ask you to explain the causes of change or evaluate the importance of one event or tactic. Use precise dates, laws and names and weigh different factors.

Exam tip: When judging significance, compare the event with others and explain what changed because of it, not only what happened.

flashcards.back: Laws in the southern US that enforced racial segregation and limited Black voting rights after the Civil War.
Supreme Court ruling that racially segregated public schools were unconstitutional.
381-day boycott (1955–56) after Rosa Parks's arrest; ended bus segregation and made Martin Luther King Jr. famous.
Nine Black students who integrated Central High School; Eisenhower sent federal troops to enforce the law.
Protest tactic begun at Greensboro in February 1960 where activists sat at whites-only counters; led to the formation of SNCC.
28 August 1963 demonstration of about 250,000 people; King's 'I Have a Dream' speech.
Banned segregation in public places and discrimination in employment on grounds of race, colour, religion, sex or origin.
Outlawed discriminatory voting tests and allowed federal supervision of voter registration; followed the Selma marches.
Malcolm X (assassinated 1965) stressed Black pride and self-defence; Black Power and the Black Panthers (1966) reflected frustration with slow change.

subject: history
subTopic: Apartheid and Resistance in South Africa

questions.content: What does the word 'apartheid' mean in the South African context?
options: A system of racial segregation and white minority rule
questions.explanation: Apartheid, meaning 'apartness' in Afrikaans, was a system of legal racial separation and discrimination introduced after 1948.

questions.content: Which party won the 1948 election in South Africa and began formal apartheid?
questions.explanation: The National Party, supported by Afrikaner voters, won in 1948 and passed apartheid laws.

questions.content: Who was the leader of the African National Congress who became South Africa's first democratically elected president in 1994?
questions.explanation: Mandela was released in 1990 after about 27 years in prison and won the election of 1994.

questions.content: What was the Sharpeville event of March 1960?
options: Police killed protesters who were demonstrating against the pass laws
questions.explanation: On 21 March 1960 police opened fire on a crowd, killing 69 people. It led to the banning of the ANC and PAC.

questions.content: Which year saw South Africa's first election open to all races?
questions.explanation: The election of 27 April 1994 ended apartheid rule and produced a government led by Mandela.

questions.content: Under the Pass Laws, Black South Africans had to carry documents. What was their main purpose?
options: To control movement and keep Black people out of white areas except as workers
questions.explanation: Passes restricted where people could live and work and allowed the police to arrest those without the right papers.

questions.content: The Group Areas Act (1950) divided cities into zones for different races. What was a major consequence?
options: Communities such as District Six in Cape Town were destroyed as people were forcibly moved
People chose where to live freely
questions.explanation: Forced removals moved non-white people to distant townships, breaking up long-established communities.

questions.content: A fictional government spent 600 rand per white pupil and 50 rand per Black pupil each year. What is the ratio of spending on white to Black pupils?
questions.explanation: 600 ÷ 50 = 12, so the ratio is 12 : 1. Unequal funding was a key feature of Bantu Education.

questions.content: The Soweto uprising began on 16 June 1976. What triggered it?
options: A requirement that some school subjects be taught in Afrikaans, as well as wider anger at Bantu Education
questions.explanation: Students protested against Afrikaans as a language of instruction. Police shot at the children, and unrest spread across the country.

questions.content: Mandela and other leaders were sentenced to life imprisonment at the Rivonia Trial in 1964. What was a consequence?
options: Resistance inside the country was weakened for a time, but Mandela became an international symbol
questions.explanation: The trial removed key leaders and the ANC was banned, yet Mandela's imprisonment on Robben Island made him a symbol of resistance.

questions.content: Why did the ANC and the PAC turn from purely peaceful protest after Sharpeville?
options: Peaceful protest had been met with violence, and both organisations were banned, so some members formed armed wings
questions.explanation: After the ban, the ANC formed Umkhonto we Sizwe (1961) and the PAC formed Poqo, turning to sabotage and armed struggle.

questions.content: Which international pressure helped weaken apartheid?
options: Sporting and economic sanctions, and boycotts
questions.explanation: South Africa was banned from the Olympic Games and many countries imposed sanctions in the 1980s, which damaged the economy and reputation.

questions.content: In 1952 the ANC and its allies ran the Defiance Campaign, in which volunteers deliberately broke apartheid rules and accepted arrest. What was the aim?
options: To overwhelm the courts and prisons and show mass opposition through non-violent action
To win a seat in parliament
questions.explanation: The campaign used peaceful civil disobedience and greatly increased ANC membership, though the government responded with harsher laws.

questions.content: Steve Biko promoted Black Consciousness. Which of his ideas is most accurate?
options: Black people should build pride and self-reliance and free their minds from feelings of inferiority
Black people should leave South Africa
Black people should wait for white leaders to act
questions.explanation: Biko influenced the Soweto generation. He died in police custody in September 1977, which caused international outrage.

questions.content: Which combination best explains why apartheid ended in the early 1990s?
options: Internal resistance, international sanctions, economic problems and a new leader, F. W. de Klerk, willing to negotiate
A change of ruling party to the ANC in 1980
questions.explanation: No single cause was enough. De Klerk unbanned the ANC and released Mandela in February 1990, and negotiations led to the 1994 election.

questions.content: Mandela was released in February 1990, having served about 27 years. Which interpretation best reflects why the government freed him?
options: The government faced growing unrest, sanctions and economic pressure and saw negotiation as necessary
He completed his sentence of 27 years exactly
questions.explanation: Mandela had a life sentence. His release was a political decision made when the costs of continuing repression were too high.

questions.content: The Truth and Reconciliation Commission (1996), chaired by Desmond Tutu, offered amnesty to those who confessed political crimes. What is the main criticism?
options: Some victims felt perpetrators avoided punishment and justice was not served
It was run by the apartheid government
questions.explanation: Supporters argued it helped the nation face the truth and avoid civil war. Critics said amnesty denied justice, so there are two sides.

questions.content: A source: an apartheid-era government pamphlet states that 'separate development' benefits every group. What is the best way to judge its reliability?
options: Accept it because it is official
Recognise that its purpose was to justify government policy, and compare it with evidence from those affected
questions.explanation: Propaganda is useful as evidence of official ideas, but its purpose limits its reliability. Cross-checking is the key skill.

note:
## What was apartheid?
Apartheid means 'apartness' in Afrikaans. After the National Party won the 1948 election, South Africa's white minority government introduced laws to separate people by race and to keep power and wealth with whites. People were classified as white, Black African, Coloured or Indian.

## Key apartheid laws
- **Population Registration Act (1950).** Classified every person by race.
- **Group Areas Act (1950).** Created separate residential areas. Whole communities, such as District Six in Cape Town, were forcibly removed.
- **Pass Laws.** Black South Africans had to carry passes to enter white areas, which controlled movement and labour.
- **Bantu Education Act (1953).** Created a separate and inferior school system.

## Resistance
- **Early protest.** The ANC organised the Defiance Campaign in 1952 and, in 1955, supporters adopted the Freedom Charter, which called for equal rights.
- **Sharpeville (21 March 1960).** Police shot at a crowd protesting against pass laws, killing 69 people. The government banned the ANC and the Pan Africanist Congress (PAC). The ANC formed an armed wing, Umkhonto we Sizwe, in 1961.
- **Rivonia Trial (1963–64).** Nelson Mandela and other leaders were sentenced to life in prison and sent to Robben Island.
- **Black Consciousness and Soweto.** Steve Biko promoted pride and self-reliance. On 16 June 1976 schoolchildren in Soweto protested against being taught in Afrikaans, and police fired on them. Biko died in police custody in 1977.
- **1980s.** The United Democratic Front (1983), strikes, township protests and states of emergency (1985–86) increased pressure.

## International pressure and the end of apartheid
The UN criticised apartheid, and sporting bans and sanctions affected South Africa's economy and reputation. In 1989 F. W. de Klerk became president. In February 1990 he unbanned the ANC and released Mandela, who had served about 27 years. Negotiations followed, and in April 1994 the first election open to all races produced a government led by Mandela. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission (1996), chaired by Desmond Tutu, investigated crimes and offered amnesty in return for full confession.

## Common mistakes
- Saying Mandela was released because his sentence ended. He had a life sentence.
- Treating apartheid as ending in one moment. It was a process from 1990 to 1994.
- Ignoring internal resistance and focusing only on foreign pressure.

## How this is examined
Typical eAssessment tasks give you a source, such as a photograph, a pass book, a speech or a government statement, and ask you to analyse its origin and purpose, then judge its value and limitation. Extended tasks might ask how far sanctions, rather than internal resistance, ended apartheid, or ask you to explain the significance of Sharpeville or Soweto. Always support your answer with dates and examples.

Exam tip: Separate the causes of apartheid's end into internal, international and individual factors, then rank them and justify your ranking.

flashcards.back: System of legal racial segregation and white minority rule introduced by the National Party after 1948; ended in the early 1990s.
Created separate residential zones for racial groups and led to forced removals, such as District Six.
Required Black South Africans to carry passes to control their movement and keep them out of white areas.
21 March 1960: police killed 69 protesters against pass laws; the ANC and PAC were banned afterwards.
1963–64 trial in which Mandela and others were sentenced to life imprisonment on Robben Island.
16 June 1976 student protest against Afrikaans in schools; police fired on children and unrest spread nationally.
Black Consciousness leader who promoted pride and self-reliance; died in police custody in September 1977.
President from 1989 who unbanned the ANC and freed Mandela in February 1990, beginning negotiations.
First election open to all races on 27 April 1994; Mandela became president. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission followed in 1996.

subject: history

questions.content: What does the word 'suffrage' mean?
options: The right to own property only
The right to a free education
questions.explanation: Suffrage is the right to vote in political elections. Women's suffrage campaigns demanded this for women.

questions.content: Which country was the first self-governing nation to give women the right to vote in national elections, in 1893?
questions.explanation: New Zealand gave women the vote in 1893, though Māori and Pākehā women were both included.

questions.content: Who founded the Women's Social and Political Union (WSPU) in 1903?
questions.explanation: Emmeline Pankhurst, with her daughters, led the more militant suffragettes under the slogan 'Deeds not words'.

questions.content: Which group, led by Millicent Fawcett, used peaceful, constitutional methods to campaign for the vote in Britain?
questions.explanation: The National Union of Women's Suffrage Societies used petitions, meetings and lobbying, in contrast to the WSPU's militancy.

questions.content: In which year was the 19th Amendment, giving women the vote across the United States, ratified?
questions.explanation: The 19th Amendment was ratified in August 1920, although many Black women in the South still faced barriers to voting.

questions.content: Why did the suffragettes adopt militant tactics such as window-smashing and arson?
options: They believed peaceful methods had failed to achieve results and wanted publicity
They wanted to start a civil war
They opposed the vote for women
The government had already given them the vote
questions.explanation: After years of peaceful campaigning without success, the WSPU moved to direct action. This split opinion, with some thinking it harmed their cause.

questions.content: Emily Wilding Davison died in June 1913 after being hit by the king's horse at the Epsom Derby. How did the event affect the movement?
options: It gave the suffragettes a martyr and increased publicity, but also divided public opinion
It resulted in an immediate law granting votes
questions.explanation: Her funeral drew huge crowds. The effects on public opinion were mixed, so historians avoid claiming it directly gave women the vote.

questions.content: In 1913 the British government passed the 'Cat and Mouse Act'. What did it allow?
options: Hunger-striking prisoners to be released and re-arrested once they had recovered
Women to vote in local elections
questions.explanation: The government wanted to avoid suffragettes dying in prison, which would create martyrs. Force-feeding had caused public anger.

questions.content: How did the First World War help women win the vote in Britain?
options: Women took on essential war work, which changed attitudes, and suffrage campaigns were suspended in favour of the war effort
Women were conscripted into the army
The government was forced to by suffragette bombings in 1916
questions.explanation: Women worked in factories, transport and farming. The Representation of the People Act 1918 gave the vote to women over 30 who met property conditions.

questions.content: In 1918 British women over 30 who met certain property conditions gained the vote. Equal voting rights with men (age 21) came in 1928. How many years after New Zealand's 1893 reform was this?
questions.explanation: 1928 − 1893 = 35 years. This shows suffrage developed at different times in different countries.

questions.content: The Representation of the People Act 1918 gave all men over 21 the vote but only some women, those over 30. What is the most likely reason for the age difference?
options: Politicians feared women voters would outnumber men after the war losses and wanted to limit the change
Women under 30 were not allowed to read
The Act applied only to Scotland
questions.explanation: Many men had died in the war. Setting the age at 30 and adding conditions limited the number of new women voters to a minority.

questions.content: A historian argues that war work alone did not win the vote; the earlier campaigns made it impossible for politicians to ignore women. What is this an example of?
options: An argument about the combination of causes
A statement of fact with no interpretation
questions.explanation: Historians often argue that the suffrage campaigns and wartime changes both contributed. Good answers consider how causes interact.

questions.content: Which of the following was a source of women's war work between 1914 and 1918 that supporters of suffrage later pointed to?
questions.explanation: Women filled jobs in munitions factories, transport and farming while men fought. This challenged beliefs that women were unsuited to public life.

questions.content: Switzerland gave women the federal vote in 1971, and the USA did so in 1920. How many years apart were these?
questions.explanation: 1971 − 1920 = 51 years. It shows that progress was uneven, even in wealthy democracies.

questions.content: Many historians distinguish 'first-wave' feminism (focused on the vote) from 'second-wave' feminism of the 1960s and 1970s. What did the second wave mainly campaign for?
options: Equal pay, workplace equality, and control over reproduction and family life
The end of the Cold War
questions.explanation: Writers such as Betty Friedan (The Feminine Mystique, 1963) challenged ideas about women's roles. Laws such as Britain's Sex Discrimination Act 1975 followed.

questions.content: A student says: 'The vote ended all inequality for women.' Which evidence most strongly challenges this claim?
options: Women continued to earn less than men, faced barriers to certain jobs and later needed equal pay and discrimination laws
questions.explanation: The vote was a milestone, but legal and social equality needed further campaigns, such as the Equal Pay Act 1970 (in force 1975) in Britain.

questions.content: In the US, the 19th Amendment did not guarantee voting for all women. Which group faced the biggest continued barriers in the South?
options: Black women, under Jim Crow voting restrictions
questions.explanation: Literacy tests, poll taxes and intimidation prevented many Black women voting until the Voting Rights Act of 1965.

questions.content: Evaluate: 'The militant methods of the suffragettes were more effective than the peaceful methods of the suffragists.' Which judgement is best supported?
options: Militancy kept the issue in the news but also alienated some supporters, while peaceful work built broad support, so effectiveness is debated
questions.explanation: Good answers weigh both gains and costs and use evidence, such as the 1918 reform that came after war work and years of both types of campaigning.

note:
## Why did women campaign for the vote?
In the nineteenth century women in most countries could not vote, hold most public offices or, in many cases, control property after marriage. Campaigners argued that women were citizens who paid taxes and were affected by laws, so they should have a say. Early international landmarks included the Seneca Falls Convention in the United States (1848) and New Zealand's decision to give women the vote in 1893.

## Suffragists and suffragettes in Britain
- **Suffragists.** The National Union of Women's Suffrage Societies (NUWSS), led by Millicent Fawcett, used peaceful methods such as petitions, meetings and lobbying.
- **Suffragettes.** Emmeline Pankhurst founded the Women's Social and Political Union (WSPU) in 1903 with the motto 'Deeds not words'. After years of little progress they used militant tactics: breaking windows, arson and hunger strikes in prison. The government responded with force-feeding and, in 1913, the 'Cat and Mouse Act'.
- **Emily Wilding Davison** died in June 1913 after stepping in front of the king's horse at the Epsom Derby. Her funeral was attended by huge crowds.

## The First World War and 1918
In 1914 the suffragettes suspended their campaign to support the war effort. Women worked in factories, transport, farms and hospitals, and attitudes changed. The Representation of the People Act 1918 gave the vote to women over 30 who met property conditions, and to all men over 21. Equal voting age with men (21) came in 1928.

## Other countries
New Zealand (1893) was first among self-governing countries. Germany and Russia gave votes to women in 1918 and 1917, the United States ratified the 19th Amendment in 1920, France in 1944, and Switzerland (federal level) in 1971. Many Black women in the American South were blocked from voting until the Voting Rights Act of 1965.

## Women's rights after the vote
The vote did not bring equality. In the 1960s and 1970s the second wave of feminism campaigned for equal pay, equal opportunities and control over family life. Betty Friedan's The Feminine Mystique (1963) questioned traditional roles. Laws followed, including the Equal Pay Act (1963) in the US, Title IX (1972) in US education, and Britain's Equal Pay Act (1970, in force 1975) and Sex Discrimination Act (1975).

## Common mistakes
- Using 'suffragist' and 'suffragette' as if they were the same.
- Saying all women won the vote in 1918. Only some did.
- Claiming war work alone won the vote and ignoring earlier campaigning.

## How this is examined
In the eAssessment you may be given a poster, a newspaper extract or a photograph and asked to explain its origin, purpose and message, then to judge its value and limitation. Longer tasks ask you to compare suffragist and suffragette methods or to evaluate the importance of the First World War. Use dates and examples, and reach a judgement.

Exam tip: When comparing methods, state what each achieved and what each risked, then say which you think was more effective and why.

Peaceful campaigners for women's votes, mainly the NUWSS led by Millicent Fawcett.
Members of the WSPU, founded by Emmeline Pankhurst in 1903, who used militant direct action under the motto 'Deeds not words'.
Allowed hunger-striking suffragettes to be released and re-arrested after recovering, to avoid creating martyrs.
Suffragette who died in June 1913 after being struck by the king's horse at the Epsom Derby.
Gave the vote to women over 30 meeting property conditions and to all men over 21.
British women gained the vote on equal terms with men, at age 21.
New Zealand 1893; Britain 1918 (partial) and 1928; USA 1920; France 1944; Switzerland (federal) 1971.
